name: Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)
summary: The ratio of cumulative traded value to cumulative volume over a horizon. The standard benchmark for judging institutional execution quality.
definition: VWAP is the average price of all trades over a period, with each trade weighted by its size. It equals total traded value divided by total traded volume.
formula:
VWAP = Σᵢ pᵢ·vᵢ / Σᵢ vᵢ

pᵢ : price of trade i        (bar data: typical price (H + L + C) / 3)
vᵢ : volume of trade i
Σ  : over all trades in the horizon (usually one session, reset at the open)

Execution cost vs. VWAP (bps) = side × (P̄_fill − VWAP) / VWAP × 10⁴
side = +1 for buys, −1 for sells; positive = worse than benchmark

sections.heading: Institutional usage
sections.html:
• Execution benchmark. Brokers and buy-side trading desks report slippage against interval VWAP. Beating VWAP on a buy means the average fill came in below it.
  • VWAP algorithms. These split a parent order across the day in proportion to a forecast intraday volume profile, so the fills track the market's own VWAP. The main risk is a bad volume forecast.
  • Intraday signal. Price relative to running VWAP is a common mean-reversion and trend filter. Anchored VWAP measures from a chosen event, such as earnings or a gap.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Bar-based VWAP built from typical price only approximates trade-level VWAP. Use tick data when the result is used for cost attribution.
  • Decide whether opening and closing auctions are included. On A-share markets the 09:15–09:25 call auction and the 14:57–15:00 closing auction can carry significant volume.
  • A large order is part of the VWAP it is measured against. Participation above roughly 10–20% of volume makes the benchmark easy to "beat" and less informative; compare with arrival price as well.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def vwap(price: pd.Series, volume: pd.Series) -> float:
    """Session VWAP: sum(p * v) / sum(v)."""
    v = volume.astype(float)
    return float((price * v).sum() / v.sum())

def intraday_vwap(bars: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Running VWAP that resets each trading day.
    bars: DatetimeIndex, columns high, low, close, volume."""
    tp = (bars["high"] + bars["low"] + bars["close"]) / 3.0  # typical price
    pv = tp * bars["volume"]
    day = bars.index.normalize()
    return pv.groupby(day).cumsum() / bars["volume"].groupby(day).cumsum()

def slippage_bps(avg_fill: float, bench_vwap: float, side: int) -> float:
    """Execution cost vs VWAP in basis points. side=+1 buy, -1 sell.
    Positive = worse than VWAP."""
    return side * (avg_fill - bench_vwap) / bench_vwap * 1e4

faq.question: Is VWAP the same as TWAP?
faq.answer: No. TWAP weights every time interval equally; VWAP weights by traded volume, so it follows the market's intraday volume curve.

test:
import pandas as pd
assert abs(vwap(pd.Series([10, 11, 12.]), pd.Series([100, 200, 700])) - 11.6) < 1e-12
assert abs(slippage_bps(10.02, 10.0, 1) - 20) < 1e-9 and abs(slippage_bps(9.98, 10.0, -1) - 20) < 1e-9

name: Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)
summary: Net buy-minus-sell pressure at the best bid and ask, measured from changes in top-of-book prices and sizes. Short-horizon price changes are approximately linear in OFI.
definition: Order Flow Imbalance aggregates every event at the best quotes (limit orders, cancellations and market orders) into one signed number. Demand added at the bid or supply removed from the ask counts as positive; supply added at the ask or demand removed from the bid counts as negative.
formula:
Per-event contribution (Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov, 2014):

eₙ =  1{Pᴮₙ ≥ Pᴮₙ₋₁}·qᴮₙ − 1{Pᴮₙ ≤ Pᴮₙ₋₁}·qᴮₙ₋₁
    − 1{Pᴬₙ ≤ Pᴬₙ₋₁}·qᴬₙ + 1{Pᴬₙ ≥ Pᴬₙ₋₁}·qᴬₙ₋₁

OFIₖ = Σ eₙ   over events n in interval k

Price impact:  ΔPₖ ≈ βₖ · OFIₖ + εₖ,   βₖ ∝ 1 / average depth

Pᴮ, qᴮ : best bid price and size     Pᴬ, qᴬ : best ask price and size

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.html:
• When the bid price is unchanged, the bid term reduces to the change in bid size. A rising bid counts the full new size, and a falling bid subtracts the full old size. The ask side mirrors this with the sign flipped.
  • The original study on US equities reports that a single linear OFI regression explains a large share of short-interval mid-price variance. It also finds that the impact coefficient scales inversely with market depth.

sections.heading: Institutional usage
sections.html:
• Short-horizon alpha and quote-skewing signals for market makers.
  • Execution: pausing or accelerating child orders when OFI runs against the order.
  • Multi-level OFI, computed over the top N levels, adds information beyond level 1 in deeper books.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Snapshot data such as the 3-second L2 snapshots common in A-share feeds hides intermediate events, so OFI computed from snapshots is a coarse approximation.
  • Normalise by average depth or volume before comparing OFI across stocks.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def ofi(book: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Per-event order flow imbalance e_n (Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov, 2014).
    book: rows are successive top-of-book snapshots with columns
          bid_px, bid_sz, ask_px, ask_sz.
    Sum e_n over a time window to get OFI for that window."""
    bp, bq = book["bid_px"], book["bid_sz"]
    ap, aq = book["ask_px"], book["ask_sz"]
    bp0, bq0, ap0, aq0 = bp.shift(), bq.shift(), ap.shift(), aq.shift()
    e = (np.where(bp >= bp0, bq, 0.0) - np.where(bp <= bp0, bq0, 0.0)
         - np.where(ap <= ap0, aq, 0.0) + np.where(ap >= ap0, aq0, 0.0))
    e = pd.Series(e, index=book.index)
    e.iloc[0] = 0.0  # no previous snapshot
    return e

# Window OFI, e.g. 10-second buckets:
# ofi_10s = ofi(book).resample("10s").sum()

faq.question: Can OFI be computed from trade data alone?
faq.answer: No. OFI needs best bid/ask prices and sizes. Trade-only data gives trade-sign imbalance (buy volume minus sell volume), a related but different measure.

name: Hurst Exponent (H)
summary: A scaling exponent that measures long-range dependence in a time series. H < 0.5 indicates mean reversion, H = 0.5 a random walk, and H > 0.5 a persistent, trending series.
definition: The Hurst exponent H describes how the spread of a process grows with the time horizon. For a series with Hurst exponent H, the typical size of a move over τ steps scales as τᴴ. A random walk has H = 0.5.
formula:
Rescaled range (R/S) on returns xₜ, window length n:
  Yₜ = Σ_{s≤t} (xₛ − x̄)            cumulative deviation
  R(n) = max Yₜ − min Yₜ ,  S(n) = std(x)
  E[R(n)/S(n)] ∝ nᴴ   →  H = slope of log(R/S) vs log n

Lagged-difference scaling on log prices pₜ:
  std(pₜ₊τ − pₜ) ∝ τᴴ   →  H = slope of log std vs log τ

H < 0.5 anti-persistent (mean-reverting)
H = 0.5 uncorrelated increments (random walk)
H > 0.5 persistent (trending)

sections.heading: Institutional usage
sections.html:
• Statistical arbitrage. A pair or basket spread with H well below 0.5 is a candidate for mean-reversion trading. Use it alongside, not instead of, a cointegration or ADF test.
  • Regime filters. A rolling H separates trending from choppy periods for momentum versus reversal strategies.
  • Volatility research. Realised-volatility series show H around 0.1, the "rough volatility" finding of Gatheral, Jaisson and Rosenbaum (2018).

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• R/S must be applied to returns, not price levels. Applied to a price series, it returns values near 1 that mean nothing.
  • Classical R/S is biased upward in small samples. On 4,096 i.i.d. normal returns the code below returns about 0.55, not 0.50. Use the Anis-Lloyd/Peters correction or DFA, and compare against a shuffled-series baseline.
  • Estimates are noisy and sensitive to the range of window sizes. Report confidence intervals, for example from a block bootstrap, before trading on a value of 0.45.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np

def hurst_rs(returns, min_n: int = 16) -> float:
    """Hurst exponent by rescaled-range (R/S) analysis.
    Input: a series of returns/increments, NOT price levels."""
    x = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    N = len(x)
    sizes = np.unique(np.floor(np.logspace(np.log10(min_n),
                                           np.log10(N // 2), 20)).astype(int))
    rs = []
    for n in sizes:
        k = N // n
        seg = x[: k * n].reshape(k, n)
        dev = np.cumsum(seg - seg.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True), axis=1)
        R = dev.max(axis=1) - dev.min(axis=1)
        S = seg.std(axis=1, ddof=0)
        ok = S > 0
        rs.append(np.mean(R[ok] / S[ok]))
    H, _ = np.polyfit(np.log(sizes), np.log(rs), 1)
    return float(H)

def hurst_lag_var(log_price, max_lag: int = 100) -> float:
    """Hurst from scaling of lagged differences: std(x[t+tau]-x[t]) ~ tau^H.
    Input: log price levels."""
    x = np.asarray(log_price, dtype=float)
    lags = np.arange(2, max_lag)
    tau = [np.std(x[l:] - x[:-l]) for l in lags]
    H, _ = np.polyfit(np.log(lags), np.log(tau), 1)
    return float(H)

faq.question: What Hurst value indicates mean reversion?
faq.answer: H below 0.5. Values near 0.5 are consistent with a random walk; small deviations are often estimator bias rather than tradable structure.

test:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); r = rng.standard_normal(4096)
assert 0.5 < hurst_rs(r) < 0.6 and 0.45 < hurst_lag_var(np.cumsum(r)) < 0.55

name: Information Coefficient (IC)
summary: The cross-sectional correlation between a factor's values and subsequent asset returns. Rank IC, its mean and ICIR are the standard first test of whether an alpha factor predicts returns.
definition: The information coefficient is the correlation, computed across assets on one date, between a factor's values and the returns those assets earn over the following holding period. Rank IC uses Spearman rank correlation, which is robust to outliers. A factor is judged on the time series of its IC: its mean, its stability (ICIR) and its statistical significance.
formula:
IC_t      = corr( f_{i,t} , r_{i,t→t+h} )        across assets i on date t
Rank IC_t = corr( rank f_{i,t} , rank r_{i,t→t+h} )   (Spearman)

Mean IC   = (1/n) Σ_t IC_t
ICIR      = mean(IC) / std(IC)
t-stat    ≈ ICIR · √(n / h)        h-period overlapping returns, n dates

Fundamental law (Grinold):  IR ≈ IC · √breadth

sections.heading: Institutional usage
sections.html:
• Factor screening. Rank IC is the first filter in most factor libraries. As a rough guide for daily-rebalanced equity factors, a mean rank IC of 0.02–0.05 with ICIR above about 0.5 is worth further work, subject to turnover and costs.
  • Decay analysis. Computing IC for horizons h = 1, 5, 10, 20 shows how fast a signal decays, which sets the rebalance frequency.
  • Factor weighting. Rolling mean IC or ICIR is a common input to dynamic factor weighting and to the expected-return scaling in mean-variance optimisation.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Look-ahead. Forward returns must start after the signal is known. For A-shares, a factor computed at the close of t can only be traded at t+1 because of T+1 settlement and order timing, so the code defaults to lag=1.
  • Untradeable names. Suspended stocks, and A-share stocks that open at limit-up (for buys) or limit-down (for sells), should be masked out. Otherwise IC overstates what can actually be captured.
  • Overlapping horizons. With h > 1 consecutive IC values share returns, so the naive t-stat is inflated. Use the √(n/h) adjustment shown here or Newey-West standard errors.
  • Size and industry exposure. A factor that is mostly a small-cap or sector bet will show high IC in some regimes. Neutralise against size and industry before judging it.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def forward_returns(close: pd.DataFrame, horizon: int = 1, lag: int = 1) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Forward return aligned to the signal date.
    close: dates x assets. A signal computed at the close of t is traded at t+lag
    (lag=1 suits A-share T+1 execution) and held for `horizon` periods."""
    return close.shift(-lag - horizon) / close.shift(-lag) - 1

def information_coefficient(factor: pd.DataFrame, fwd_ret: pd.DataFrame,
                            method: str = "rank", min_obs: int = 20) -> pd.Series:
    """Cross-sectional IC per date, fully vectorised (no per-date loop).
    method="rank" gives Spearman rank IC; "pearson" gives normal IC."""
    f, r = factor.align(fwd_ret, join="inner")
    valid = f.notna() & r.notna()
    f, r = f.where(valid), r.where(valid)
    if method == "rank":
        f, r = f.rank(axis=1), r.rank(axis=1)
    f = f.sub(f.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    r = r.sub(r.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    ic = (f * r).sum(axis=1) / np.sqrt((f ** 2).sum(axis=1) * (r ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    return ic.where(valid.sum(axis=1) >= min_obs)

def ic_summary(ic: pd.Series, horizon: int = 1) -> dict:
    """Mean IC, ICIR and an approximate t-stat. Overlapping horizons share
    information, so the effective sample size is taken as n / horizon."""
    ic = ic.dropna()
    n, m, s = len(ic), ic.mean(), ic.std(ddof=1)
    return {"n": n, "mean_ic": m, "ic_std": s, "icir": m / s,
            "t_stat": m / s * np.sqrt(n / horizon), "hit_rate": (ic > 0).mean()}

faq.question: What is a good IC value?
faq.answer: For daily or weekly equity factors, a mean rank IC around 0.03–0.05 is typically considered meaningful, and ICIR above 0.5 indicates a stable signal. Values much higher than 0.1 on broad universes usually point to look-ahead bias or a data error.

faq.question: Should I use rank IC or Pearson IC?
faq.answer: Rank IC is the default because it is robust to outliers and to the non-normal cross-section of returns. Pearson IC is closer to what a linear model captures and is useful when factor values are already standardised and winsorised.

test:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
rng = np.random.default_rng(1); a = rng.standard_normal((30, 200)); r = 0.05 * a + rng.standard_normal((30, 200))
ic = information_coefficient(pd.DataFrame(a), pd.DataFrame(r))
assert max(abs(ic[t] - spearmanr(a[t], r[t]).statistic) for t in range(30)) < 1e-12
assert forward_returns(pd.DataFrame({"a": [10, 11, 12, 13.]}))["a"].iloc[0] == 12 / 11 - 1

name: Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test
summary: A unit-root test that checks whether a time series is non-stationary. In stat-arb it is the standard check that a spread mean-reverts before it is traded.
definition: The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test asks whether a series has a unit root, meaning shocks never decay and the series wanders like a random walk. The null hypothesis is a unit root (non-stationary). A sufficiently negative test statistic rejects it in favour of a stationary, mean-reverting series. Lagged differences are added to the regression to absorb serial correlation.
formula:
Δy_t = α + β·t + γ·y_{t−1} + Σ_{i=1..p} δ_i·Δy_{t−i} + ε_t

H0: γ = 0 (unit root)     H1: γ < 0 (stationary)
ADF statistic = γ̂ / se(γ̂)     → compare with Dickey-Fuller (MacKinnon) critical values,
                                  NOT Student-t
Large-sample critical values, constant only:  1% −3.43   5% −2.86   10% −2.57

Mean-reversion half-life (from Δy_t = a + g·y_{t−1}):  HL = ln 2 / −ln(1 + g)

sections.heading: Institutional usage
sections.html:
• Pairs and basket spreads. A spread is traded only if ADF rejects a unit root. The half-life then sets the holding period and the look-back for the rolling mean and standard deviation of the z-score.
  • Model hygiene. Regressing one non-stationary series on another gives spurious R² and t-stats. Test levels first, and difference or use cointegration methods when a unit root is present.
  • Feature engineering. Testing candidate features for stationarity before feeding them to ML models avoids features whose distribution drifts out of the training range.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Low power. With a few hundred observations, ADF often cannot tell a slowly mean-reverting series (AR coefficient 0.98) from a random walk. Failing to reject is not evidence of a unit root. Pair it with KPSS, whose null is the reverse.
  • Deterministic terms matter. Including a trend when there is none, or omitting one that exists, shifts the critical values and the conclusion. Use "c" for spreads and "ct" only for trending series.
  • Structural breaks. A level shift, such as a regime change or an index inclusion, makes a stationary series look non-stationary (Perron, 1989).
  • Estimated spreads. If the series is a regression residual, ordinary ADF p-values are too optimistic. Use residual-based critical values: see cointegration.
  • Multiple testing. Screening thousands of A-share pairs at 5% yields hundreds of false positives. Adjust the threshold, or require out-of-sample confirmation.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

def adf_stat(y, lags: int = 1) -> float:
    """ADF t-statistic with a constant, by plain OLS (for understanding).
    Regression: dy_t = a + g*y_{t-1} + sum_{i=1..lags} b_i*dy_{t-i} + e_t ;  returns t(g)."""
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    dy = np.diff(y)
    T = len(dy) - lags
    X = [np.ones(T), y[lags:-1]]
    X += [dy[lags - i:-i] for i in range(1, lags + 1)]
    X = np.column_stack(X)
    target = dy[lags:]
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, target, rcond=None)
    resid = target - X @ beta
    s2 = resid @ resid / (T - X.shape[1])
    se = np.sqrt(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)[1, 1])
    return float(beta[1] / se)

def adf_test(y, regression: str = "c") -> dict:
    """Production test: lag order by AIC and MacKinnon p-values via statsmodels.
    regression: "c" constant, "ct" constant + trend, "n" none."""
    y = np.asarray(y, float)
    try:   # statsmodels >= 0.15 lets us pin the classic tuple return
        res = adfuller(y, regression=regression, autolag="AIC", result_object=False)
    except TypeError:
        res = adfuller(y, regression=regression, autolag="AIC")
    return {"stat": res[0], "pvalue": res[1], "lags": res[2], "nobs": res[3], "crit": res[4]}

def half_life(y) -> float:
    """Mean-reversion half-life in periods from dy_t = a + g*y_{t-1}: ln(2) / -ln(1+g).
    Returns inf if the series is not mean-reverting (g >= 0)."""
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y) - 1), y[:-1]])
    g = np.linalg.lstsq(X, np.diff(y), rcond=None)[0][1]
    return float(np.log(2) / -np.log1p(g)) if g < -1e-10 else float("inf")
test:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
x = np.zeros(1000)
for t in range(1, 1000): x[t] = 0.95 * x[t-1] + rng.standard_normal()
for L in (1, 3):
    assert abs(adf_stat(x, L) - adfuller(x, maxlag=L, autolag=None, regression="c")[0]) < 1e-9
assert adf_test(x)["pvalue"] < 0.01
assert adf_test(np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(1000)))["pvalue"] > 0.05
assert 8 < half_life(x) < 30 and half_life(np.arange(100.0)) == float("inf")

faq.question: What is the difference between the ADF and KPSS tests?
faq.answer: They reverse the hypotheses. ADF's null is a unit root (non-stationary); KPSS's null is stationarity. Rejecting ADF and failing to reject KPSS together is the strongest evidence of stationarity; conflicting results usually mean the sample is too short or the series is near a unit root.

faq.question: Which p-value threshold should I use for pairs selection?
faq.answer: 5% is conventional for a single test, but screening many pairs inflates false discoveries. Use a stricter threshold such as 1%, a false-discovery-rate correction, or confirm stationarity on a later out-of-sample window before trading.

name: Cointegration (Engle-Granger & Johansen)
summary: Two or more non-stationary price series are cointegrated when some linear combination of them is stationary. This is the statistical basis of pairs and basket trading.
definition: Cointegration means that individually non-stationary series share a common stochastic trend, so a weighted combination of them (the spread) is stationary and mean-reverts. The Engle-Granger two-step method tests one pair through a regression residual. The Johansen method tests several series at once and estimates how many independent cointegrating relationships exist.
formula:
Engle-Granger (two steps):
  1. y_t = α + β·x_t + u_t            (OLS; β = hedge ratio)
  2. ADF on û_t with residual-based MacKinnon critical values
     (2 series, constant: 1% −3.90   5% −3.34   10% −3.04)

Johansen (VECM):
  Δy_t = Π·y_{t−1} + Σ_{i=1..k} Γ_i·Δy_{t−i} + ε_t ,   rank(Π) = r cointegrating vectors
  Trace statistic for H0: rank ≤ r :  λ_trace(r) = −T · Σ_{i=r+1..n} ln(1 − λ̂_i)

sections.heading: Institutional usage
sections.html:
• Pairs trading. Go long the spread when its z-score is low and short when it is high. Size the legs with the hedge ratio β.
  • Basket and index arbitrage. Johansen finds stationary portfolios across three or more assets, for example an ETF against its largest constituents.
  • Cross-market spreads. Examples include A/H dual-listed shares, futures calendar spreads, and commodity crack or crush spreads.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Wrong p-values. Running a plain ADF on an estimated residual overstates significance, because OLS already minimised the residual variance. In the test for this page, an unrelated pair gets p = 0.11 from plain ADF but p = 0.27 from the correct residual-based test.
  • Asymmetry. Regressing y on x and x on y give different hedge ratios and can give different conclusions. Johansen is symmetric.
  • Unstable hedge ratios. A β estimated once drifts over time. Re-estimate on a rolling window, or let β vary with a Kalman filter.
  • Correlation is not cointegration. Two stocks can have highly correlated returns yet drift apart without bound in price.
  • A-share implementation. Short legs depend on margin-lending availability (融券), which is limited and was further restricted from 2023. Many A-share pair strategies are therefore run as long-only relative-value switches or hedged with index futures.

code_snippet:
import warnings
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint
from statsmodels.tsa.vector_ar.vecm import coint_johansen

def engle_granger(y, x) -> dict:
    """Two-step Engle-Granger test of y ~ a + b*x.
    Uses residual-based MacKinnon critical values (statsmodels.coint), NOT the
    ordinary ADF p-value, which is too lenient for an estimated spread."""
    y, x = np.asarray(y, float), np.asarray(x, float)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])
    (a, b), *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    stat, p, crit = coint(y, x, trend="c", autolag="AIC")
    return {"alpha": a, "hedge_ratio": b, "spread": y - a - b * x,
            "stat": stat, "pvalue": p, "crit": crit}

def johansen(prices, det_order: int = 0, k_ar_diff: int = 1) -> dict:
    """Johansen trace test for an (T x n) price matrix.
    det_order: -1 none, 0 constant, 1 trend. Returns the cointegration rank
    at 95% and the first cointegrating vector (normalised on asset 0)."""
    with warnings.catch_warnings():  # recent NumPy: harmless ComplexWarning inside statsmodels
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore", np.exceptions.ComplexWarning)
        res = coint_johansen(np.asarray(prices, float), det_order, k_ar_diff)
    trace, cv95 = res.lr1, res.cvt[:, 1]
    rank = 0
    while rank < len(trace) and trace[rank] > cv95[rank]:
        rank += 1
    vec = np.real(res.evec[:, 0] / res.evec[0, 0])
    return {"rank": rank, "trace": trace, "cv95": cv95, "weights": vec}
test:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
x = np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(1500)) + 50
y = 2 + 1.5 * x + rng.standard_normal(1500)
z = np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(1500))
eg = engle_granger(y, x)
assert abs(eg["hedge_ratio"] - 1.5) < 0.01 and eg["pvalue"] < 0.01
assert engle_granger(z + 50, x)["pvalue"] > 0.05
j = johansen(np.column_stack([y, x, z]))
assert j["rank"] == 1 and abs(j["weights"][1] + 1.5) < 0.02 and abs(j["weights"][2]) < 0.05

faq.question: Should I use Engle-Granger or Johansen?
faq.answer: Engle-Granger is simple and fine for a single pair, but its result depends on which series is the dependent variable and it finds at most one relationship. Johansen handles three or more series, is symmetric and estimates the number of cointegrating vectors, at the cost of sensitivity to lag length and deterministic-term choices.

faq.question: How is cointegration different from correlation?
faq.answer: Correlation measures co-movement of returns over a window; cointegration is about the price levels staying tied together over time. Highly correlated stocks can drift apart permanently, while cointegrated ones are pulled back to an equilibrium spread.

name: Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES)
summary: VaR is the loss threshold that is exceeded only with a given small probability. Expected Shortfall is the average loss in that tail. Both are standard risk limits; ES is what Basel FRTB uses for market risk capital.
definition: Value at Risk at confidence level α is the loss that is not exceeded with probability α over a given horizon. Expected Shortfall (also called CVaR) is the average loss given that the loss exceeds VaR. ES therefore accounts for how bad the tail is, not only where it starts. Unlike VaR, it is a coherent risk measure (subadditive).
formula:
VaR_α = −q_{1−α}(r)                         (q = quantile of returns)
ES_α  = −E[ r | r ≤ q_{1−α}(r) ]

Normal:          VaR = −(μ + σ·z),   ES = −(μ − σ·φ(z)/(1−α)),   z = Φ⁻¹(1−α)
Cornish-Fisher:  z_cf = z + (z²−1)S/6 + (z³−3z)K/24 − (2z³−5z)S²/36
                 (S = skewness, K = excess kurtosis)

Kupiec POF backtest (x exceptions in n days, p = 1−α, p̂ = x/n):
  LR = −2·ln[ (1−p)^{n−x} p^x / ((1−p̂)^{n−x} p̂^x) ]  ~ χ²(1)

sections.heading: Institutional usage
sections.html:
• Risk limits and reporting. Daily 99% VaR is the classic desk limit. Basel FRTB replaced it with 97.5% ES for market-risk capital because ES captures tail severity.
  • Backtesting. Regulators and risk teams count VaR exceptions and run the Kupiec test. Too many exceptions mean the model understates risk.
  • Strategy evaluation. Historical VaR and ES of a backtest's daily returns are reported alongside Sharpe and max drawdown. The performance calculator computes them from a pasted equity curve.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Normal VaR understates fat tails. On simulated Student-t (4 degrees of freedom) returns, 99% normal VaR is 3.26% against a historical 3.75%, and normal ES misses by even more (3.74% against 5.12%).
  • Cornish-Fisher can overshoot. The expansion is only valid for moderate skew and kurtosis. On the same t(4) sample it gives 6.03%, far above the true quantile. Prefer historical or filtered-historical methods for heavy tails.
  • Sample size. A 99% historical VaR from 250 days rests on about 2.5 observations. Use longer windows, or 97.5% ES, which averages more points.
  • √h scaling. Multiplying 1-day VaR by √10 assumes i.i.d. returns. Volatility clustering and autocorrelation break it.
  • A-share price limits. The ±10% daily limit (±20% on ChiNext and STAR, ±5% for ST) truncates observed daily losses. Consecutive limit-down days then produce multi-day losses far beyond the 1-day historical VaR.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm, chi2

def var_es(returns, alpha: float = 0.99, method: str = "historical") -> tuple:
    """One-period VaR and Expected Shortfall as positive loss fractions.
    method: "historical" | "normal" | "cornish-fisher" (skew/kurtosis-adjusted
    quantile; returns ES = nan because the expansion defines no tail mean)."""
    r = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    r = r[~np.isnan(r)]
    if method == "historical":
        q = np.quantile(r, 1 - alpha)
        return -q, -r[r <= q].mean()
    mu, sd = r.mean(), r.std(ddof=1)
    z = norm.ppf(1 - alpha)
    if method == "normal":
        return -(mu + sd * z), -(mu - sd * norm.pdf(z) / (1 - alpha))
    if method == "cornish-fisher":
        # VaR only: CF adjusts the quantile, it does not define a tail mean.
        x = (r - mu) / sd
        s, k = np.mean(x ** 3), np.mean(x ** 4) - 3
        zc = z + (z**2 - 1) * s / 6 + (z**3 - 3*z) * k / 24 - (2*z**3 - 5*z) * s**2 / 36
        return -(mu + sd * zc), float("nan")
    raise ValueError(method)

def kupiec_pof(returns, var_series, alpha: float = 0.99) -> dict:
    """Kupiec proportion-of-failures backtest. var_series: forecast VaR (positive)
    made BEFORE each return. H0: exception rate = 1 - alpha."""
    r, v = np.asarray(returns, float), np.asarray(var_series, float)
    n, x, p = len(r), int((r < -v).sum()), 1 - alpha
    ph = x / n
    ll0 = (n - x) * np.log(1 - p) + x * np.log(p)
    ll1 = (0.0 if x == n else (n - x) * np.log(1 - ph)) + (0.0 if x == 0 else x * np.log(ph))
    lr = -2 * (ll0 - ll1)
    return {"n": n, "exceptions": x, "expected": n * p, "lr": lr, "pvalue": 1 - chi2.cdf(lr, 1)}
test:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
r = rng.standard_normal(200000) * 0.01 + 0.0005
tv, te = -(0.0005 + 0.01 * norm.ppf(0.01)), -(0.0005 - 0.01 * norm.pdf(norm.ppf(0.01)) / 0.01)
for m in ("historical", "normal"):
    v, e = var_es(r, 0.99, m)
    assert abs(v - tv) < 3e-4 and abs(e - te) < 3e-4, m
v, e = var_es(r, 0.99, "cornish-fisher"); assert abs(v - tv) < 3e-4 and np.isnan(e)
k = kupiec_pof(rng.standard_normal(2000) * 0.01, np.full(2000, 0.015))
assert k["pvalue"] < 0.01 and k["exceptions"] > k["expected"]
assert kupiec_pof(np.zeros(10), np.ones(10))["exceptions"] == 0

faq.question: Should I use 95%, 99% or 97.5%?
faq.answer: 99% one-day VaR is the traditional trading-desk limit and Basel VaR standard; 97.5% ES is the Basel FRTB standard and is roughly comparable in level to 99% VaR under normality while being more stable to estimate. 95% is common for strategy reporting because it has more tail observations.

faq.question: Why is Expected Shortfall preferred to VaR?
faq.answer: VaR says nothing about losses beyond the threshold and is not subadditive, so combining two portfolios can show higher VaR than the sum of their VaRs. ES averages the whole tail and is coherent, which makes it better for limits and capital allocation.

name: Amihud Illiquidity Measure (ILLIQ)
summary: The average absolute return per unit of traded value: how much the price moves for each yuan or dollar traded. It is a low-frequency price-impact proxy and a widely used liquidity factor.
definition: Amihud (2002) illiquidity is the average, over a window of days, of the absolute daily return divided by the day's traded value. A high value means small amounts of trading move the price a lot. It needs only daily returns and turnover, so it can be computed for every stock over long histories. That makes it the standard low-frequency liquidity measure in asset-pricing research.
formula:
ILLIQ_{i,T} = (1 / D_{i,T}) · Σ_{d ∈ T} |r_{i,d}| / VOLD_{i,d}  × scale

r_{i,d}    : daily return of stock i
VOLD_{i,d} : traded value that day (A-shares: 成交额 in yuan, not 成交量 in shares)
D_{i,T}    : number of valid trading days in window T (zero-turnover days excluded)
scale      : e.g. 10⁸ → |return| per 100 million yuan traded

sections.heading: Institutional usage
sections.html:
• Liquidity factor. Illiquid stocks earn a return premium in many markets, and Amihud ILLIQ is the usual sort variable. It is a common factor in A-share multi-factor models, often in log form.
  • Capacity and cost estimates. ILLIQ times the planned trade size gives a rough expected price move. This is used to cap position sizes in small-cap strategies.
  • Universe filters. Excluding the most illiquid decile before backtesting avoids returns that could never be captured at scale.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Use value, not volume. Dividing by share volume makes a ¥5 stock look far more liquid than a ¥500 stock with the same yuan turnover.
  • Suspensions. Zero-turnover days give infinite ratios. The code drops them and requires a minimum number of valid days.
  • Price-limit days. A stock that is locked at limit-up shows about a 10% move on tiny turnover, which creates extreme ILLIQ values. Winsorise, or exclude limit-locked days, and note that ChiNext and STAR moved to ±20% limits, so mixed-regime histories are not directly comparable.
  • Skew. The cross-section spans several orders of magnitude. Use log(ILLIQ) or ranks in regressions and factor models.
  • Size proxy. ILLIQ is strongly correlated with market cap. Neutralise against size before claiming a separate liquidity effect.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def amihud(ret: pd.DataFrame, amount: pd.DataFrame, window: int = 20,
           min_days: int = 15, scale: float = 1e8) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Rolling Amihud illiquidity, dates x stocks, fully vectorised.
    ILLIQ = mean(|r_t| / amount_t) * scale over the window.
    amount: traded value in currency (A-shares: yuan turnover, 成交额), so with
    scale=1e8 the result reads as |return| per 100 million yuan traded.
    Zero-amount days (suspensions) are excluded rather than producing inf."""
    a = amount.where(amount > 0)
    daily = ret.abs() / a
    return daily.rolling(window, min_periods=min_days).mean() * scale

def amihud_monthly(ret: pd.DataFrame, amount: pd.DataFrame, scale: float = 1e8) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Original Amihud (2002) style: average within each calendar month."""
    daily = ret.abs() / amount.where(amount > 0)
    return daily.groupby(daily.index.to_period("M")).mean() * scale
test:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
d = pd.bdate_range("2024-01-01", periods=60)
R = pd.DataFrame(rng.standard_normal((60, 3)) * 0.02, d, list("abc"))
A = pd.DataFrame(rng.uniform(1e7, 1e9, (60, 3)), d, list("abc")); A.iloc[10:15, 1] = 0
il = amihud(R, A)
ref = np.mean([abs(R.iloc[t, 1]) / A.iloc[t, 1] for t in range(40, 60)]) * 1e8
assert abs(il.iloc[59, 1] - ref) < 1e-15 and np.isfinite(il.iloc[24, 1])
assert amihud_monthly(R, A).shape == (3, 3)

faq.question: Why take the log of Amihud illiquidity?
faq.answer: Raw ILLIQ is extremely right-skewed: the most illiquid stocks can be thousands of times the median. Log or rank transforms keep a few outliers from dominating regressions, factor portfolios and IC calculations.

faq.question: Monthly or rolling window?
faq.answer: The original paper averages within each calendar month or year. A rolling 20-day window updates daily and suits trading signals; use at least 15 valid days so suspensions do not produce noisy values.

name: Fast Rolling Mean, Std, Beta and Z-score with Numba
summary: O(n) rolling mean, standard deviation, OLS beta and 2-D z-score compiled with Numba. In tests here they run 4 to 7 times faster than pandas and are more accurate on large-valued series.
definition: These functions compute rolling statistics with running sums in a single compiled pass, instead of recomputing each window. Values are re-centred on the first window's mean, which avoids the catastrophic cancellation that running sums suffer on series with large levels, such as prices or index points. Numba compiles plain Python loops to machine code, so there is no build step: install with pip and call the functions on NumPy arrays.
formula:
Running sums over the window, after centring v = x − c:
  S₁ += v_new − v_old       S₂ += v_new² − v_old²
  mean = S₁/w + c            var = (S₂ − w·(S₁/w)²) / (w − 1)
  beta = (S_xy − S_x·S_y/w) / (S_xx − S_x²/w)

Measured here, 1,000,000 points, window 250 (mean + std + beta):  Numba ≈ 20 ms, pandas ≈ 135 ms
2,000 × 500 matrix, rolling z-score, window 60:                   Numba ≈ 11 ms, pandas ≈ 52 ms
Max relative std error vs exact two-pass:                         Numba 1.6e−9, pandas 2.2e−8

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.html:
• Long minute-bar or tick series where pandas rolling is the bottleneck.
  • Rolling hedge ratios for pairs, and rolling z-scores across a whole stock universe in one call.
  • Inside larger Numba-compiled backtest loops, since these functions can be called from other @njit code.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• NaN handling. The inputs must be NaN-free. Running sums propagate a NaN forever. Fill, drop or split around gaps first.
  • Compile time. The first call compiles, which takes about a second. cache=True stores the compiled code next to the file so later runs start instantly.
  • Numerical drift. Without centring, the variance of a series around 10,000 loses most of its significant digits. If the level changes enormously over the sample, re-centre periodically.
  • Parallelism. For very wide matrices, switch the column loop in rolling_zscore_2d to numba.prange with parallel=True.

code_snippet:
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit(cache=True)
def rolling_mean_std(x, window):
    """O(n) rolling mean and sample std (ddof=1) with running sums.
    Values are re-centred on the first window's mean to limit cancellation error.
    NaN where fewer than `window` observations; input must contain no NaN."""
    n = x.shape[0]
    mean = np.full(n, np.nan)
    std = np.full(n, np.nan)
    if n < window:
        return mean, std
    shift = x[:window].mean()
    s = 0.0
    s2 = 0.0
    for i in range(n):
        v = x[i] - shift
        s += v
        s2 += v * v
        if i >= window:
            o = x[i - window] - shift
            s -= o
            s2 -= o * o
        if i >= window - 1:
            m = s / window
            mean[i] = m + shift
            var = (s2 - window * m * m) / (window - 1)
            std[i] = np.sqrt(var) if var > 0 else 0.0
    return mean, std

@njit(cache=True)
def rolling_beta(y, x, window):
    """Rolling OLS slope cov(y, x) / var(x), O(n). Use for hedge ratios or market beta.
    Inputs are re-centred on their first-window means to limit cancellation error."""
    n = y.shape[0]
    out = np.full(n, np.nan)
    if n < window:
        return out
    cx = x[:window].mean()
    cy = y[:window].mean()
    sx = sy = sxx = sxy = 0.0
    for i in range(n):
        a = x[i] - cx
        b = y[i] - cy
        sx += a; sy += b; sxx += a * a; sxy += a * b
        if i >= window:
            a = x[i - window] - cx
            b = y[i - window] - cy
            sx -= a; sy -= b; sxx -= a * a; sxy -= a * b
        if i >= window - 1:
            cov = sxy - sx * sy / window
            var = sxx - sx * sx / window
            if var > 0:
                out[i] = cov / var
    return out

@njit(cache=True)
def rolling_zscore_2d(X, window):
    """Rolling z-score for every column of a (T x N) float matrix, in one compiled pass."""
    T, N = X.shape
    Z = np.full((T, N), np.nan)
    for j in range(N):
        m, s = rolling_mean_std(X[:, j].copy(), window)
        for i in range(T):
            if s[i] > 0:
                Z[i, j] = (X[i, j] - m[i]) / s[i]
    return Z
test:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
x = rng.standard_normal(20000).cumsum() + 1e4
y = 0.7 * x + rng.standard_normal(20000)
m, s = rolling_mean_std(x, 250); b = rolling_beta(y, x, 250)
X, Y = pd.Series(x), pd.Series(y)
assert np.nanmax(np.abs(m - X.rolling(250).mean())) < 1e-8
assert np.nanmax(np.abs(s - X.rolling(250).std()) / X.rolling(250).std()) < 1e-6
i = 12345; ex = np.polyfit(x[i-249:i+1], y[i-249:i+1], 1)[0]
assert abs(b[i] - ex) < 1e-8 and np.isnan(b[248]) and not np.isnan(b[249])
M = rng.standard_normal((300, 20)).cumsum(0)
D = pd.DataFrame(M)
assert np.nanmax(np.abs(rolling_zscore_2d(M, 60) - ((D - D.rolling(60).mean()) / D.rolling(60).std()).values)) < 1e-8

faq.question: Why Numba instead of Cython?
faq.answer: Numba needs no compiler toolchain or build step: decorate a function and it is compiled on first call. Performance for simple numeric loops is comparable to Cython, and the code stays plain Python that can be copied and run directly.

faq.question: Is pandas rolling not already fast?
faq.answer: pandas rolling is implemented in Cython and is fine for most work, but each statistic is a separate pass with object overhead, and combinations such as rolling beta need several calls. A single fused Numba pass was 4–7× faster in the benchmarks above.

name: Query Tick Data in Parquet with DuckDB
summary: Build 1-minute OHLCV and VWAP bars, and daily turnover, straight from Hive-partitioned tick Parquet files with DuckDB. There is no database server and no loading step, and filters skip unneeded files and row groups.
definition: DuckDB is an in-process analytical database that queries Parquet files in place. With one folder per trading day (Hive partitioning), a date filter skips whole folders. Sorting rows by stock code inside each file lets Parquet's row-group min/max statistics skip most of the data for a code filter. The snippet shows the storage layout, a writer that produces it, and queries for minute bars and daily turnover.
formula:
Layout:  ticks/date=YYYY-MM-DD/part-0.parquet   (ts, seq, code, price, volume)

read_parquet('ticks/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
  WHERE date BETWEEN ? AND ?      → partition pruning (folders never opened)
    AND code IN (...)             → row-group pruning via min/max statistics

open  = arg_min(price, (ts, seq))      close = arg_max(price, (ts, seq))
vwap  = Σ price·volume / Σ volume       bucket = time_bucket(INTERVAL 1 MINUTE, ts)

sections.heading: Why this layout
sections.html:
• One partition per day matches how tick data arrives and how research queries are scoped. Adding a day means writing one new folder.
  • Sorted by code, zstd-compressed. This gives small files and effective code filters. Avoid thousands of tiny files: aim for one to a few files per day.
  • The same files are readable by pandas, Polars and Spark, so there is no lock-in.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Timestamp ties. Several ticks often share one timestamp. Ordering by ts alone picked the wrong open or close in 27–30% of minutes in the test for this page. Always carry the exchange sequence number and order by (ts, seq).
  • Auction ticks. A-share opening (09:15–09:25) and closing (14:57–15:00) call-auction prints are single-price matches. Decide whether bars include them, and filter by time if not.
  • Time zones. Store exchange-local timestamps consistently, either naive local time or TIMESTAMPTZ, but never mixed.
  • Partition column type. Hive values are parsed from folder names. Compare against values of the same type, and check with DESCRIBE.

code_snippet:
import duckdb

# Layout this snippet assumes (Hive partitioning, one folder per trading day):
#   ticks/date=2024-03-01/part-0.parquet    columns: ts TIMESTAMP, seq BIGINT, code VARCHAR, price DOUBLE, volume BIGINT
# seq = exchange sequence number. Several ticks often share one timestamp, so open/close
# must be ordered by (ts, seq); ordering by ts alone picks an arbitrary tick on ties.
#   ticks/date=2024-03-04/part-0.parquet    ...

def connect(threads: int = 0) -> duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection:
    con = duckdb.connect()                      # in-memory; Parquet stays on disk
    if threads:
        con.execute(f"SET threads = {threads}")
    return con

def minute_bars(con, root: str, codes: list, start: str, end: str):
    """1-minute OHLCV + VWAP straight from tick Parquet.
    The date filter prunes whole partition folders and the code filter is pushed down
    to Parquet row-group statistics, so only the needed bytes are read."""
    return con.execute(f"""
        SELECT code,
               time_bucket(INTERVAL 1 MINUTE, ts)   AS minute,
               arg_min(price, (ts, seq))             AS open,
               max(price)                            AS high,
               min(price)                            AS low,
               arg_max(price, (ts, seq))             AS close,
               sum(volume)                           AS volume,
               sum(price * volume) / sum(volume)     AS vwap
        FROM read_parquet('{root}/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
        WHERE date BETWEEN ? AND ? AND code IN (SELECT unnest(?))
        GROUP BY ALL
        ORDER BY code, minute
    """, [start, end, codes]).df()

def daily_turnover(con, root: str, start: str, end: str):
    """Per-stock daily traded value, e.g. the 'amount' input for the Amihud measure."""
    return con.execute(f"""
        SELECT date, code, sum(price * volume) AS amount
        FROM read_parquet('{root}/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
        WHERE date BETWEEN ? AND ?
        GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY date, code
    """, [start, end]).df()

def write_partitioned(con, df, root: str):
    """Write a pandas DataFrame with a 'date' column as Hive-partitioned, zstd Parquet,
    sorted by code so row-group min/max statistics make code filters effective."""
    con.register("src", df)
    con.execute(f"""COPY (SELECT * FROM src ORDER BY date, code, ts, seq)
                    TO '{root}' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (date), COMPRESSION zstd, OVERWRITE_OR_IGNORE)""")
    con.unregister("src")
test:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, tempfile, os
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
days = pd.bdate_range("2024-03-01", periods=3); n = 30000
df = pd.DataFrame({"date": np.repeat(days.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"), n // 3),
    "ts": (pd.to_datetime(np.repeat(days, n // 3)) + pd.to_timedelta(34200 + np.tile(np.sort(rng.integers(0, 7200, n // 3)), 3), unit="s")).values,
    "seq": np.arange(n), "code": rng.choice(["600000", "600519", "000001"], n),
    "price": rng.uniform(10, 11, n).round(2), "volume": rng.integers(1, 100, n) * 100})
root = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "ticks")
con = connect(); write_partitioned(con, df, root)
bars = minute_bars(con, root, ["600519"], "2024-03-04", "2024-03-05")
sub = df[(df.date >= "2024-03-04") & (df.code == "600519")].sort_values(["ts", "seq"])
sub = sub.assign(minute=sub.ts.dt.floor("min"))
g = sub.groupby("minute").agg(open=("price", "first"), close=("price", "last"), volume=("volume", "sum")).reset_index()
m = bars.merge(g, on="minute", suffixes=("", "_pd"))
assert len(m) == len(g) == len(bars)
assert (m.open == m.open_pd).all() and (m.close == m.close_pd).all() and (m.volume == m.volume_pd).all()
assert np.isclose(daily_turnover(con, root, "2024-03-01", "2024-03-05").amount.sum(), (df.price * df.volume).sum())

faq.question: Why DuckDB instead of loading everything into pandas?
faq.answer: DuckDB reads only the partitions, columns and row groups a query needs, runs multi-threaded, and spills to disk when data exceeds memory. Tens of millions of ticks that would not fit comfortably in a pandas DataFrame can be aggregated directly from Parquet.

faq.question: Should I store ticks in a .duckdb file or in Parquet?
faq.answer: Both work. Parquet is open, portable across pandas/Polars/Spark and easy to append by day; a .duckdb database file is convenient for derived tables and indexes. A common pattern is raw ticks in partitioned Parquet and derived bars or factors in a DuckDB file.

name: Vectorised Daily Backtest with A-share Trading Constraints
summary: A daily long-only backtest core that vectorises over the whole stock universe. It blocks look-ahead by construction and handles suspensions, limit-up and limit-down untradability and turnover costs. A Polars version is included for the unconstrained case.
definition: The backtest turns a dates × stocks boolean signal into equal-weight holdings and daily net returns. Every operation is vectorised across stocks. Only the loop over dates remains, because whether a stock can be bought or sold today depends on what is already held: a stock stuck at limit-down cannot be sold and stays in the book. Orders decided at the close of day t execute at the close of t+1, so a signal can never use the return it trades on.
formula:
Timing:   signal[t] (data ≤ close t) → order at close t+1 → earns close(t+1) → close(t+2)

want_t    = signal_{t−1}
held_t    = enter if want ∧ ¬held ∧ buyable_t ;  exit if ¬want ∧ held ∧ sellable_t
weight_t  = held_t / Σ held_t
gross_t   = Σ_i weight_{t−1,i} · r_{t,i}
turnover_t= Σ_i |weight_{t,i} − weight_{t−1,i}|
net_t     = gross_t − turnover_t · cost_bps / 10⁴

sections.heading: What the tests check
sections.html:
• Net returns match a naive per-stock, per-day loop to within 1e−17.
  • The Polars version matches the pandas version when every stock is tradable.
  • Look-ahead probe. Two hypothetical signals were run. One uses only the next day's return, which this timing can never capture; it earns about zero (0.03% per day, which is noise). The other uses the return two days ahead, which this timing does capture; it earns 1.6% per day, the size of gain that look-ahead leaks would produce.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.html:
• Costs. A-share stamp duty is charged on sells only (0.05% since 28 August 2023), plus commission and slippage. A single symmetric cost_bps is an approximation; use separate buy and sell rates for precision.
  • Prices. Use dividend- and split-adjusted closes, such as back-adjusted 后复权 prices, or returns will show false jumps.
  • Survivorship. Include delisted stocks and the universe as it was on each date, not today's constituents.
  • Close execution is optimistic. Trading exactly at the close ignores closing-auction impact. Stress-test with next-day VWAP or open execution.
  • Tradability flags. Derive limit-up and limit-down from the previous close and the board's limit (±10% main board, ±20% ChiNext/STAR, ±5% ST). A close at the limit price is the usual proxy for "could not trade in that direction".

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def backtest(signal: pd.DataFrame, close: pd.DataFrame, tradable_buy: pd.DataFrame,
             tradable_sell: pd.DataFrame, cost_bps: float = 15.0) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Daily long-only, equal-weight backtest, dates x stocks, no Python loop over assets.

    signal[t]        : True = want to hold, decided with data up to the close of t
    tradable_buy[t]  : can buy at the close of t   (A-shares: not suspended, not at limit-up)
    tradable_sell[t] : can sell at the close of t  (not suspended, not at limit-down)
    Orders for signal[t] execute at the close of t+1; returns are close-to-close.
    cost_bps is charged on one-way turnover (commission + stamp duty + slippage)."""
    want = signal.shift(1).fillna(False).astype(bool)          # no look-ahead
    held = np.zeros(signal.shape[1], dtype=bool)
    hold = np.zeros(signal.shape, dtype=bool)
    tb, ts, w = tradable_buy.to_numpy(bool), tradable_sell.to_numpy(bool), want.to_numpy(bool)
    for t in range(len(signal)):                                # loop over dates only
        held = np.where(w[t] & ~held & tb[t], True, held)       # enter if allowed
        held = np.where(~w[t] & held & ts[t], False, held)      # exit if allowed (else stuck)
        hold[t] = held
    n = hold.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    weight = pd.DataFrame(np.divide(hold, n, out=np.zeros(hold.shape), where=n > 0),
                          index=signal.index, columns=signal.columns)
    ret = close.pct_change(fill_method=None).fillna(0.0)
    gross = (weight.shift(1).fillna(0.0) * ret).sum(axis=1)      # weight set at close t earns t+1
    turnover = weight.diff().abs().sum(axis=1).fillna(weight.abs().sum(axis=1))
    net = gross - turnover * cost_bps / 1e4
    return pd.DataFrame({"gross": gross, "turnover": turnover, "net": net,
                         "equity": (1 + net).cumprod(), "n_held": n.ravel()})

def backtest_polars(signal_long, cost_bps: float = 15.0):
    """Polars version for the simple case (always tradable) on long data with columns
    date, code, close, signal. Same timing convention as backtest()."""
    import polars as pl
    df = (signal_long.sort("code", "date")
          .with_columns(want=pl.col("signal").shift(1).over("code").fill_null(False),
                        ret=(pl.col("close") / pl.col("close").shift(1) - 1).over("code").fill_null(0.0))
          .with_columns(n=pl.col("want").sum().over("date"))
          .with_columns(weight=pl.when(pl.col("n") > 0).then(pl.col("want").cast(pl.Float64) / pl.col("n")).otherwise(0.0))
          .with_columns(w_prev=pl.col("weight").shift(1).over("code").fill_null(0.0)))
    daily = (df.group_by("date").agg(gross=(pl.col("w_prev") * pl.col("ret")).sum(),
                                     turnover=(pl.col("weight") - pl.col("w_prev")).abs().sum())
             .sort("date")
             .with_columns(net=pl.col("gross") - pl.col("turnover") * cost_bps / 1e4))
    return daily.with_columns(equity=(1 + pl.col("net")).cum_prod())

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, polars as pl
rng = np.random.default_rng(9); T, N = 120, 15
d = pd.bdate_range("2024-01-01", periods=T); c = [f"s{i}" for i in range(N)]
close = pd.DataFrame(np.exp(np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal((T, N)) * 0.02, 0)) * 10, d, c)
sig = pd.DataFrame(rng.random((T, N)) < 0.3, d, c)
tb = pd.DataFrame(rng.random((T, N)) > 0.1, d, c); ts = pd.DataFrame(rng.random((T, N)) > 0.1, d, c)
res = backtest(sig, close, tb, ts, 15)
held, prev, rets, net = set(), dict.fromkeys(c, 0.0), close.pct_change(fill_method=None).fillna(0), []
for t in range(T):
    want = sig.iloc[t-1] if t else pd.Series(False, index=c)
    for k in c:
        if want[k] and k not in held and tb.iloc[t][k]: held.add(k)
        if not want[k] and k in held and ts.iloc[t][k]: held.discard(k)
    w = {k: (1 / len(held) if k in held else 0.0) for k in c}
    net.append(sum(prev[k] * rets.iloc[t][k] for k in c) - sum(abs(w[k] - prev[k]) for k in c) * 15 / 1e4); prev = w
assert np.max(np.abs(np.array(net) - res.net.values)) < 1e-12
allT = pd.DataFrame(True, d, c); r2 = backtest(sig, close, allT, allT, 15)

lg.columns = ["date", "code", "close", "signal"]
assert np.max(np.abs(backtest_polars(pl.from_pandas(lg), 15)["net"].to_numpy() - r2.net.values)) < 1e-12

faq.question: Why is there still a loop over dates?
faq.answer: Holdings are path-dependent once trading constraints exist: a stock at limit-down cannot be sold, so whether it is held today depends on yesterday's holdings. The loop runs over dates only, with every operation inside vectorised across the whole universe, so a 20-year daily backtest on 5,000 stocks is about 5,000 vectorised steps.

faq.question: How do I avoid look-ahead bias?
faq.answer: Shift every signal by at least one period before it can affect positions, and decide the execution price in advance. In this code a signal formed at the close of t trades at the close of t+1 and first earns the t+1 to t+2 return; the test suite checks that a signal built from the t to t+1 return earns nothing.
